journal: JOURNAL OF PARK AND RECREATION ADMINISTRATION
title: An Examination of the Guided Night Hiking Experience in Parks and Protected Areas
setting: recreation (guided night hikes on park and forest trails: a strenuous 3-mile hike at Table Rock State Park and an easy 'owl prowl' at Congaree National Park, South Carolina, and a moderately difficult 1.5-mile hike at Pisgah National Forest, North Carolina; ranger interviews also from Acadia National Park, Maine)
design: qualitative (phenomenological semi-structured interviews with night hikers and interpretive rangers; verbatim transcription, open and axial coding after Miles & Huberman 1994 and Strauss & Corbin 1998; triangulation and informant checks)
sample_n: 35 interviewees (31 night hikers - Table Rock 10, Congaree 11, Pisgah 10 - plus 4 interpretive rangers; hiker interviews averaged 17 min, range 9-39 min; ranger interviews averaged 33 min, range 17-53 min)
exposure: In-situ night-time acoustic environment of guided hikes, described by participants rather than measured or manipulated: nocturnal natural sounds (owls, cicadas, crickets, frogs, night bugs, a distant coyote or dog, wind in the trees, a babbling creek) and the 'natural quiet' produced by less human and traffic noise at night ([page 88]-[page 89], printed pp.79-80; [page 92]-[page 93], pp.83-84). No sound level measurement, acoustic index or experimental sound manipulation is reported. Reverse side: the recreational behaviour itself - choosing to hike at night rather than by day, hiking in guided groups of 10 to 30 people, whispering when communicating, and keeping artificial lights off - is reported to shape the acoustic environment and the salience of its perception ([page 90], p.81; [page 92]-[page 93], pp.83-84).
behaviour_measure: Self-reported recreation behaviour elicited by a common semi-structured interview script: (a) participation in guided night hiking rather than day hiking, the stated motivations for it and stated willingness to hike at night again ([page 88], p.79; [page 91], p.82); (b) in-group vocal behaviour during the hike - whispering and talking less to protect natural quiet ([page 90], p.81; [page 93], p.84); (c) keeping artificial lights off and stepping 10-15 feet away from the group at stops ([page 90], p.81; [page 94], p.85). No counts, frequencies or durations are reported - the authors state that the themes 'do not represent a frequency of comments' ([page 87], p.78).
measurement_method: self-report (semi-structured interviews with 31 hikers and 4 interpretive rangers, recorded and transcribed verbatim; the lead researcher joined the hikes to build rapport but no systematic observation data are reported)
key_finding: Night soundscapes, together with the night sky, were one of the two sensory attributes that defined the night hiking experience and were raised by respondents when asked about enjoyment, favourite aspects, motivations, outcomes and willingness to hike at night again, with owls, cicadas, crickets, frogs, a distant coyote and a creek named repeatedly ([page 88]-[page 89], pp.79-80). Conversely the night activity reshaped the acoustic experience: with limited visibility hikers relied more heavily on hearing, which drew attention to both night sounds and the lack of sound, and most participants said they deliberately whispered while communicating in order to protect natural quiet, while rangers added that too much artificial light may quiet nocturnal animals ([page 93], p.84; [page 94], p.85). Quietness at night, together with limited visibility, was also the reason respondents gave for an increased sense of both group and individual solitude despite hike group sizes of 10 to 30 ([page 90], p.81).
effect_stats: NR (qualitative study; the authors state explicitly that the themes 'do not represent a frequency of comments' ([page 87], p.78) and report no counts or statistics for the sound-behaviour relation)

journal: Korea Institute of Design Research Society
title: Sound, Symbol, and Space: An Ethnosemiotic Analysis of Vernacular Soundscapes in Honghai Morning Market
setting: street (Honghai Morning Market: ca. 1 km open-air street market in a city in Northeast China, open 05:00-08:00 daily, adjacent to housing and a school)
design: qualitative (ethnosemiotic field study: repeated soundwalks, sound mapping, direct observation, photography, semi-structured interviews)
sample_n: NR (no participant count reported; unit of analysis = market sound events and three stall case studies; 11 customers recorded as attracted at the tofu stall during one 40 min 21 s recording)
exposure: Market soundscape recorded with a ZOOM H6 recorder along a fixed soundwalk route (each walk ca. 40 min, at opening, peak and pre-closure hours) and mapped as 12 representative sources from a 44 min 17 s recording, with decibel values extracted in Adobe Audition (§3-1, §3-2 [page 6-8]). Sounds were coded as performance sounds (dialect hawking calls, food-preparation sounds), navigation sounds (live poultry crowing, water splashing, defeathering machine, weighing scales) and background sounds (conversations, transaction sounds, vehicle honking, wind and bird calls). Reported acoustic features: hawking calls ca. 4 s each with rising intonation and high amplitude; high-decibel chicken crowing at 2000-4000 Hz lasting 1-2 s; defeathering machine ca. 75-85 dB running ca. 4 min per activation; blowtorch hissing at 2000-4000 Hz in 20-30 s bursts with 6-10 s intervals (§4-1 to §4-3 [page 9-12]).
behaviour_measure: Observed immediate behavioural responses to market sounds: bodily orientation adjustments (turning heads, pausing, glancing), spatial movement (approaching the sound source, altering walking paths) and initiation of social interaction (talking to companions or engaging vendors); counts of customers attracted by hawking and of immediate purchases at the tofu stall; vendors' adjustment of hawking frequency and loudness in response to foot traffic and closing time.
measurement_method: observation (direct observation 2-3 visits per week of ca. 1 h each, photography of behavioural reactions, soundwalk field notes; semi-structured interviews are declared in §1-2 and §3-1 but no interview data are reported)
key_finding: Market sounds functioned as a symbolic system that steered users' behaviour: hawking calls, poultry crowing and blowtorch noise triggered acoustic orientation (head turning, pausing), movement towards or away from the source and the start of vendor-customer interaction, and at the tofu stall hawking directly attracted 11 customers of whom 5 bought immediately. In the reverse direction, vendors shaped the soundscape strategically, raising the frequency and volume of hawking during high foot traffic and near closing time (from one call every 9-15 s to one every 3-6 s).
effect_stats: Descriptive counts only; no inferential statistics reported. Tofu stall: 24 hawking calls in 40 min 21 s, every 9-15 s during the first 15 min vs every 3-6 s during the following 25 min; hawking 'directly attracted 11 customers, five of whom made immediate purchases' (§4-1 [page 9-10]). Poultry stall: 48 high-decibel crows totalling ca. 83 s; defeathering machine activated 3 times, ca. 4 min each, ca. 75-85 dB (§4-2 [page 10]). Blowtorch stall: 42 min 17 s recording, bursts of 20-30 s at 6-10 s intervals (§4-3 [page 11]).

journal: The Science of The Total Environment
title: Effects of a human sound-based index on the soundscapes of urban open spaces
setting: mixed (Harbin, China: 4 urban parks including two squares (Children's Park, Stalin Park, Grand Theatre Square, Music Square), 2 nature parks (Sun Island Scenic Spot, Railway Bridge Park), 2 pedestrian streets (Central Street, Railway Bridge) and 1 main road (Friendship Street); 41 survey points at 9 sites, classified as human+natural (HN) or human+traffic (HT) dominant)
design: mixed (cross-sectional field campaign combining drone-photograph observation of crowd density, on-site intercept questionnaire and 10-min A-weighted sound level measurements; six 2.5-h cycles per site on a weekday and a weekend in May and October, 09:00-11:30 / 13:00-15:30 / 18:00-20:30, 18-26 degC to hold thermal sensation constant)
sample_n: 323 valid questionnaires (171 male, 152 female; ages 20-60 only: 20-30 25.4%, 30-40 36.5%, 40-50 26.3%, 50-60 11.8%) (analytic units: 41 survey points at 9 sites; crowd-density analyses use 67 respondents at 7 HN points from 42 drone photos and 56 respondents at 2 HT points from 12 drone photos, all in Children's Park)
exposure: Reverse: crowd density (mean people per 100 m2) as the behavioural exposure, counted from drone photographs of a 30 m x 30 m area divided into 1 m x 1 m grids at each survey point (§2.3, Fig. 2). Acoustic/soundscape outcomes: measured A-weighted L(A)eq, L(A)max and L(A)min (10 min per point every 15 min, GB 3096-2008, meter 1.2-1.5 m above ground, §2.5); the red soundscape index RSI from a 7-point perceived-loudness scale for human (talking, footsteps, music, children's playfulness), natural (birds, insects, water, wind) and traffic (engines, brakes, horns) sources, with RSIn = perceived human / natural and RSIt = perceived human / traffic (§2.1, Appendix); overall soundscape assessment (OSA, -3 to +3) and SSQP pleasantness, eventfulness, calmness, vibrancy (§2.4).
behaviour_measure: Crowd density (people/100 m2): average number of people inside a 30 m x 30 m area at each survey point, counted on drone photographs with a 1 m x 1 m grid overlay, taken once per 2.5-h cycle in three daily periods on a weekday and a weekend simultaneously with the questionnaire (§2.3, Figs 2-3). Crowd density was photographed only at the Children's Park points (Fig. 3 flow chart).
measurement_method: observation (drone photographs of 30 m x 30 m areas, manual counting of people on a 1 m x 1 m grid); self-report (on-site intercept questionnaire on perceived sound sources, OSA and soundscape quality). Sound level meters measured the acoustic outcome only and are not counted as behavioural sensors.
key_finding: Crowd density was significantly positively correlated with the perceived human-sound ratio (RSIn rho = 0.302, p < 0.05; RSIt rho = 0.553, p < 0.01), and RSI in turn tracked the measured sound level: A-weighted SPL rose linearly with RSIn (+8.49 dBA per unit) and fell with RSIt (-2.65 dBA per unit). Overall soundscape assessment declined linearly with RSIn in the 0.8-1.5 range - which the authors map onto crowd densities of 0.79-1.29 people/100 m2, with OSA stable at about 2.55 below 0.79 and about 1.70 above 1.29 people/100 m2 - while its relation to RSIt was an inverted parabola peaking at RSIt = 2. Sites classified as human-sound predominant had significantly higher L(A)eq and the lowest OSA, pleasantness and calmness in human+natural settings (Figs 7-10).
effect_stats: Table 1 (§3.1.1): crowd density vs RSIn Spearman = 0.302* (N = 67); crowd density vs RSIt Spearman = 0.553** (N = 56) (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01). Eq. (3) / Fig. 4(a): SPL = 8.49RSIn + 51.37, R2 = 0.657, p < 0.01, F = 61.524. Eq. (4) / Fig. 4(b): SPL = -2.65RSIt + 66.90, R2 = 0.412, p < 0.01, F = 50.687. Eq. (5) / Fig. 5: OSA = -0.86RSIn + 3.19, R2 = 0.591, p < 0.01, F = 7.129 for 0.8 <= RSIn <= 1.5 (RSIn < 0.8: R2 = 0.003, p > 0.05; RSIn > 1.5: R2 = 0.016, p > 0.05). Eq. (6) / Fig. 6: OSA = -0.53RSIt^2 + 2.13RSIt - 0.47, R2 = 0.389, p < 0.01, F = 5.930, axis of symmetry RSIt = 2.01 (1.5 < RSIt < 2.5 sub-range regression p = 0.659). Figs 7-10: Kruskal-Wallis differences in L(A)eq, OSA, pleasantness and calmness among the three perception classes (adjusted p < 0.05 / p < 0.01; exact statistics not reported).

title: Performance and atmosphere in urban public spaces: Street music in Guangzhou, China
setting: mixed (Guangzhou public spaces: riverbanks/Ersha Island, commercial streets such as Tianhe Road and Beijing Road, squares such as Tianyu Square and Grandview Plaza, and subway station forecourts at Chebei, Kecun, Tiyuxi and Lujiang)
design: mixed (participant observation with field notes and photographs + open-ended on-site questionnaire + structured and unstructured interviews + analysis of user-uploaded social media videos; fieldwork Dec 2013-Mar 2014, Xiaohongshu videos retrieved 15-30 Apr 2023)
sample_n: 200 valid audience questionnaires (203 distributed); 17 buskers (12 face-to-face, 5 online) and 3 chengguan interviewed, 400 minutes of interview data; 60 Xiaohongshu videos analysed
exposure: Live street music (busking) as an added sound source in urban public space: guitar, violin and saxophone performance whose genre, tempo, lyrics and amplification are adapted to the venue - at busy plazas and commercial streets (Grandview Plaza, Tianyu Square) buskers 'play music with faster rhythms and turn up sound amplification equipment to the maximum to occlude distracting noises' from automobiles, while at quiet venues (Ersha Island) they play comfortable pieces in line with the surrounding atmosphere (§6); ambient traffic noise, crowd noise, cheers and applause form the competing background soundscape recorded in observation (§4). Reverse side: buskers' venue selection (based on pedestrian flow and environmental noise) and performance practice reshape the acoustic quality, soundscape and 'atmosphere' of the space and, cumulatively, the perceived character of the city (§5-§7).
behaviour_measure: Stopping to listen and appreciate the performance; staying/lingering at a performance site and duration of stay; applauding, including clapping after other audience members' applause; singing along with the busker, video recording, holding up phone flashlights; donating money; formation and size of the audience crowd; buskers' choice, occupation, rotation and competition for performance venues across the city
measurement_method: self-report (open-ended questionnaire with 200 audience members and passers-by; structured/unstructured interviews with 17 buskers and 3 chengguan); observation (participant observation with field notes and photographs at Ersha Island, Grandview Plaza, Chebei subway station and Tianyu Square; content analysis of 60 Xiaohongshu videos showing audience responses)
key_finding: Street music elicited observable engagement from passers-by: about 65% of respondents said they would stop and appreciate street music if permitted, 38% said the atmosphere of the venue made them stay and listen, and 69% clapped after others had applauded, with further responses including video recording, singing along and holding up phone flashlights (§5·§7·Fig. 2). Engagement was contingent on the setting: at high-flow morning rush-hour venues (Grandview Plaza, Chebei subway station) audiences lingered only briefly and participation was low, whereas emotionally resonant performances made younger audiences 'stay longer, give more money, and applaud more sincerely' (§7). In the reverse direction, buskers' behaviour reshaped the acoustic environment - choosing venues by pedestrian flow and ambient noise, raising tempo and amplification to mask traffic noise at busy plazas and playing gentler pieces at quiet Ersha Island - so that, in the authors' account, 'a sonic affect based on loud music that attracts people's attention replaces the sonic pollutant of noisy traffic' and the acoustic quality of urban spaces is improved, with 52% of participants saying street music plays an active role in constructing the image of Guangzhou (§6·§7).
effect_stats: Descriptive percentages only; no inferential statistics or effect estimates are reported. '[A]pproximately 65% of participants said they would stop and appreciate street music, if permitted' (§5); '69% of our participants clapped their hands after the applause of others' (§5); '38% of participants said that the atmosphere made them stay and appreciate street music performances (Figure 3)' (§7); street music 'plays an active role in constructing the image of Guangzhou, according to 52% of participants' (§7); most frequently spotted venues: riverbanks 61.5%, commercial streets 32.5%, subway stations 25.0%, gardens 22.5% (§5); 37% judged the street music excellent and 25% called it free and independent and thus desirable (§5). Denominator n=200 audience questionnaires (Table 1).

title: Effects of soundscape on Chinese children?s social interaction measured by self-reported behavioral expectations
setting: VR-lab (laboratory audio-visual reproduction of one schoolyard and one urban park; 4-min videos without people projected on a 1.5 x 1.0 m screen in a 4.6 x 2.9 x 3.3 m recording studio)
design: lab-VR-experiment (within-subject laboratory experiment; eight soundscape stimuli plus a No sound control crossed with two visual environments, presented in random order)
sample_n: 38 children analysed (40 recruited, 19 boys / 19 girls, aged 6-12, grades 1-6 balanced; analytic unit: 592 condition observations, 65-66 per soundscape)
exposure: Eight soundscape stimuli built from 13 recorded sounds (Motorized transport; Human movement = run & walk; Electro-mechanical = construction & ventilation; Animal = birdsong & barking; Nature = leaves rustle & water; Children's = playing, laughter & singing; Adults' = conversation & singing; Classical music = Mozart K448 II) plus a No sound control, all reproduced at 55 dBA (+/-1 dBA) measured as LAeq,4min at the child's earhole; laboratory background 21.0-23.2 dBA; psychoacoustic indicators (FS, S, R, N) of each stimulus reported in Table 6
behaviour_measure: Self-reported behavioural expectation in three operational categories: Interaction (wants to interact with others in the place), Nonparticipation (wants to stay in the place but alone), Avoiding (does not want to stay / not come), elicited 15 s after exposure by the question 'In this place, do you want to be with other people, or be here alone, or not come?' and confirmed by a demonstration step in which the child added, positioned and connected virtual characters on the video scene and reported their sex, activity and relationship (Fig. 3-4)
measurement_method: self-report (forced-choice question plus child-led on-screen demonstration recorded by the experimenter; no observation of actual behaviour)
key_finding: Compared with the No sound control, Children's sounds (Interaction 71.2 %) and Nature sounds (63.1 %) significantly raised children's expectation to enter the place and interact (36.4 % under No sound), whereas Animal sounds (46.2 %) and Classical music (40.9 %) significantly raised the expectation to stay alone (21.2 % under No sound). Correspondence analysis associated Human movement, Children's, Adults' and Nature sounds with Interaction, Animal sounds and Classical music with Nonparticipation, and Motorized transport and Electro-mechanical sounds with Avoiding. The soundscape effect did not differ significantly between the schoolyard and the urban park, and no individual difference by sex, age, grade or personality was found.
effect_stats: Overall 3 x 9 contingency test: X2 = 152.651, p = 0.000, Cramer's V = 0.359 (Table 3, §3.1). Post hoc 2 x 2 chi-square of each soundscape vs No sound, Bonferroni adjusted alpha 0.00625 (Table 4, Fig. 5): Children's sounds X2 = 16.139, df = 2, p = 0.000; Nature sounds X2 = 17.330, p = 0.000; Classical music X2 = 24.173, p = 0.000; Animal sounds X2 = 20.519, p = 0.000; Adults' sounds X2 = 8.953, p = 0.011; Human movement sounds X2 = 6.002, p = 0.050; Electro-mechanical sounds X2 = 6.857, p = 0.032; Motorized transport sounds X2 = 4.467, p = 0.107. Correspondence analysis: dimension 1 78.83 %, dimension 2 23.17 % of variance (Table 5, Fig. 6). Stepwise multinomial logistic regression: only the soundscape main effect entered the model (X2 = 152.651, p = 0.000); visual environment and soundscape x visual environment were dropped (§3.3); interaction with sex, age, grade and personality n.s. (X2 = 24.994, p = 0.125).

title: The Impact of Auditory Traffic Perception on Pedestrians’ Street-Crossing Behavior: Insights from Real and Virtual Environments
setting: mixed (a real four-metre-wide one-way street on the campus of the Technical University of Munich, closed to public traffic and used by only a few university employees, plus a meticulously reconstructed virtual replica of the same street presented in a motion-capture VR laboratory; [page 5])
design: field-experiment (real-street experiment with a between-subjects sound condition and repeated crossings; the same participants also completed an identical lab-VR-experiment in a replica of that street, with environment order counterbalanced; §3.3 [page 6]-[page 7])
sample_n: 30 participants (19 male, 11 female; mean age 21 years, SD = 2, recruited on a university campus; 15 in the audiovisual group - 9 male, 6 female - and 15 in the sound-deprived group - 10 male, 5 female); 900 crossing trials in total (2 sound conditions x 2 environments x 15 participants x 15 repetitions) (§3.1 [page 4]-[page 5], §4 [page 7])
exposure: Presence versus absence of auditory perception of an approaching vehicle. In the real street, the sound-deprived group wore hearing protection while the other group heard the environment normally; in the virtual environment the same contrast was created by a sound-deprived visual-only setting versus a custom immersive audio display over circumaural Bose QuietComfort 25 active-noise-cancelling headphones (§3.1-3.2 [page 5]). The virtual acoustic environment combined ambient background sound of the traffic-calmed area (distant traffic, birdsong) with spatialised three-dimensional vehicle sound built from recorded engine, tire-pavement and aerodynamic components and rendered in Pure Data with propagation time, ITD, ILD, HRTF and the Doppler effect (§3.2 [page 5]-[page 6]). Approaching vehicles travelled at a constant 30, 35 or 40 km/h from about 130 m, five encounters per speed in pseudorandomised order (§3.3 [page 6]).
behaviour_measure: Shortest accepted time-to-contact (TTC) at the moment the participant judged crossing to be no longer safe: standing one step into the street, participants stepped back onto the curb, crossing a photoelectric sensor line that triggered a lidar measurement of the approaching vehicle’s exact distance and velocity; TTC = distance / velocity (§3.3 [page 6]-[page 7]). A shorter accepted TTC denotes riskier crossing behaviour.
measurement_method: sensor-GPS-video (photoelectric trigger plus lidar measurement of vehicle distance and speed at the step-back moment in the real street; simulator logging of vehicle distance and a Vicon-based full-body motion capture system with 39 markers in the virtual environment; §3.2-3.3 [page 5]-[page 7])
key_finding: Pedestrians who could not hear the approaching vehicle accepted significantly shorter time-to-contact, that is behaved more riskily, in both settings: the mean accepted TTC was 0.30 s shorter without sound in the real street and 0.28 s shorter without sound in the virtual environment, an average reduction of about 10% from the real-street baseline of 2.9 s (§4.2 [page 8], §5.1 [page 9]). The effect of removing sound was of almost identical size in the real and the virtual setting, although crossings in the virtual environment were about 25% riskier overall than in the real street (virtual TTC values were roughly 76% of the real ones), and no learning effect across the 15 repetitions was found (§4.3-4.4 [page 8]-[page 9]).
effect_stats: Linear mixed model with crossed random effects (TTC dependent, sound condition fixed, crossing sequence random, CSH covariance): real environment F(1, 28) = 4.25, p = .049; virtual environment F(1, 28) = 17.75, p < .001; mean TTC 0.30 s shorter without sound in the real environment and 0.28 s shorter without sound in the virtual environment (§4.2 [page 8]). Environment contrast by group: with sound, virtual M = 2.2 s, SD = 1.0 versus real M = 2.9 s, SD = 1.2, F(1, 28) = 132.33, p < .001; without sound, virtual M = 1.9 s, SD = 0.8 versus real M = 2.6 s, SD = 0.9, F(1, 28) = 93.37, p < .001; virtual-to-real regression F(1, 28) = 85.77, p < .001, R2 = .75, slope SE = 0.082 (§4.3 [page 8]-[page 9]). Learning-effect regressions all non-significant (e.g., real with sound F(1, 13) = 0.23, p = .640, R2 = .017; §4.4 [page 9]).
